title: Total internal reflection and optical fibers
subtitle: Trapping light when rays cannot escape

learn.prompt: Light inside acrylic (n1 = 1.49) reaches water (n2 = 1.33) at an angle of 35°. Adjust the refracted beam according to Snell's law.
learn.explanation: Because light enters a less dense medium (lower index), it speeds up and bends away from the normal line, exiting at 40.0°.

learn.prompt: What happens when light travelling inside glass (n = 1.50) hits an air boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle (41.8°)?
learn.hint: Beyond the critical angle, Snell's law yields sin(θ2) > 1, which has no real solution for refraction.
learn.explanation: No light can escape into the air. 100% of the light reflects back into the glass. This is total internal reflection (TIR).

options.label: All light is reflected internally with zero escaping into the air
The light is completely absorbed by the surface
The light refracts along the surface line at 90°
The frequency of the light doubles

misconceptionMap.b: TIR is pure reflection, not absorption; total internal reflection produces virtually no loss.
misconceptionMap.c: At exactly the critical angle light skims the surface at 90°; beyond the critical angle it reflects entirely.
misconceptionMap.d: Reflection never changes the frequency of light.

learn.prompt: A step-index optical fiber has a core (n1 = 1.50) and cladding (n2 = 1.20). The critical angle is arcsin(1.20 / 1.50) = arcsin(0.8) ≈ 53.1°. Set the slider to the critical angle in degrees.
A dense flint glass with n = 2.0 meets air (n = 1.0). Since sin(θc) = 1.0 / 2.0 = 0.5, enter the critical angle in degrees.
learn.explanation: sin(30°) = 0.5, so the critical angle is exactly 30°.

check.prompt: Can total internal reflection occur when light travels from air into glass?
check.hint: Remember which medium must have the higher refractive index for rays to bend away from normal.
check.explanation: No. Light only bends away from the normal when passing from a higher index (slower) medium to a lower index (faster) medium.

options.label: No — TIR requires light to start in the higher-index medium
Yes — if the incident angle is above 45°
Yes — but only for polarized laser light
Yes — at any grazing incidence angle

misconceptionMap.b: Entering a denser medium always bends rays toward the normal, never past 90°.
misconceptionMap.c: Polarization does not overcome Snell's boundary condition.
misconceptionMap.d: Grazing incidence into a denser medium refracts at the critical angle inside, but never reflects internally.

check.prompt: Why are telecommunication signals carried across oceans via glass fiber optics rather than copper cables?
check.hint: Consider the reflection efficiency and attenuation of total internal reflection.
check.explanation: Total internal reflection traps light pulses inside the fiber core with negligible loss over vast distances, supporting immense bandwidth.

options.label: Total internal reflection keeps optical signals trapped inside the fiber with minimal attenuation
Glass conducts electrical charges faster than copper
Light waves are immune to the speed of light limit
Fiber optic cables generate their own laser power along the path

misconceptionMap.b: Glass is an electrical insulator, not a conductor; it guides light waves.
misconceptionMap.c: Light travels at c/n in glass, which is approximately 200,000 km/s.
misconceptionMap.d: Optical fibers do not generate power; they passively guide light.

takeaway.title: Trapping light with total internal reflection
takeaway.body: When light passes from a higher-index to a lower-index medium, rays bend away from the normal. Past the critical angle sin(θc) = n2 / n1, 100% of the light reflects internally, enabling fiber optics and laser wave guides.
